title: Open Challenges for AI Engineering: Simon Willison
talk_summary: Simon Willison surveys the post-GPT-4-barrier landscape: GPT-4-class models are now a commodity across many providers, cheap small models are viable, and the hard problems are usability, trust, prompt injection, and unreviewed AI 'slop'. It is mostly a state-of-the-field and responsibility talk, not an engineering-technique talk.

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues that cheap small models (Claude 3 Haiku, Gemini 1.5 Flash) are 'incredibly inexpensive' and 'very very good', and that GPT-3.5-turbo is now both pricier and worse, so builders should move off it.
takeaways.evidence_quote: they are incredibly inexpensive they are very very good models ... if you are building there you are in the wrong place

takeaways.what_they_do: Dismisses MMLU as 'bar trivia' and points to LMSYS Chatbot Arena (blind pairwise human votes, Elo) as the best available signal for real-world model quality.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need to measure the Vibes right that's what matters when you're evaluating a model

takeaways.what_they_do: Documents the recurring bug where a chatbot renders markdown images containing private data in the URL, exfiltrating secrets to an attacker server; the fix is to not render remote markdown images.
takeaways.evidence_quote: don't render markdown images in this kind of format ... six different extremely talented teams who have made the exact same mistake

takeaways.technique: Treat LLMs as gullible; require verification of untrusted input
takeaways.what_they_do: Notes that models believe anything anyone tells them, so decisions based on unverified injected content are dangerous; also warns against publishing unreviewed AI output ('slop') and stresses human accountability.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if we think that we can trust them to make decisions based on unverified information they been ped we're just going to end up in in a huge amount of of trouble

takeaways.technique: Human accountability gate on AI output
takeaways.what_they_do: Defines 'slop' as AI content that is both unrequested and unreviewed, and argues a human must stake reputation on published output because models cannot.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you're just firing prompts into a model and then whatever comes out you're publishing it online you're part of the problem
